## 1. Dataset Selection

**(A) Citations.** I used two datasets from NOAA: the daily observations and, for the benchmark, the official
climate normals for the same station.

> Menne, M. J., Durre, I., Korzeniewski, B., McNeill, S., Thomas, K., Yin, X., Anthony, S., Ray, R., Vose, R. S.,
> Gleason, B. E., & Houston, T. G. (2012). *Global Historical Climatology Network – Daily (GHCN-Daily),
> Version 3* [Data set]. Station USC00106152, MOSCOW U OF I, ID US, daily maximum temperature (TMAX),
> January 1, 2021 – January 31, 2026. NOAA National Climatic Data Center. <https://doi.org/10.7289/V5D21VHZ>.
> Accessed September 24, 2026.

> Palecki, M., Durre, I., Applequist, S., Arguez, A., & Lawrimore, J. (2021). *U.S. Climate Normals 2020:
> U.S. Monthly Climate Normals (1991–2020)* [Data set]. Station USC00106152. NOAA National Centers for
> Environmental Information. <https://doi.org/10.25921/wck8-er13>. Accessed September 24, 2026.

Working links to the exact files I downloaded:

* [Daily observations query (NCEI Access Data Service)](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/services/data/v1?dataset=daily-summaries&stations=USC00106152&startDate=2021-01-01&endDate=2026-01-31&dataTypes=TMAX,TMIN,PRCP,SNOW&units=standard&format=csv&includeStationName=true)
* [Monthly normals query for the same station](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/services/data/v1?dataset=normals-monthly-1991-2020&stations=USC00106152&format=csv&dataTypes=MLY-TMAX-NORMAL,MLY-PRCP-AVGNDS-GE001HI)

**(B) Background.**

* **The station.** The data come from the weather station on the University of Idaho campus in Moscow. It is
  a National Weather Service **Cooperative Observer (COOP)** station. Once a day a trained observer records
  the highest and lowest temperature since the last reading. NOAA's National Centers for Environmental
  Information (NCEI) quality-checks and archives these readings in the GHCN-Daily database.
* **How the data were collected.** Nobody sampled anything: the station records *every* day, so the file is
  a complete record for one location.
* **The file.** The daily file I downloaded has one row per day from January 2021 through January 2026. I
  kept only the July days of 2021–2025, which gives **`r nrow(frame_jul)` days**. None of them are missing a
  high temperature.
* **The benchmark.** NOAA's **1991–2020 Climate Normals** are 30-year averages computed from the same
  station's records. For July, the normal daily maximum temperature (`MLY-TMAX-NORMAL`) is **84.4 °F**.

## 2. Question and Hypothesis Formulation

**(A) Question.** Were July afternoons in Moscow from 2021 to 2025 hotter, on average, than the official
1991–2020 normal of 84.4 °F?

I chose this because recent summers have felt hot. For example, the record-breaking Pacific Northwest heat
wave was in late June 2021. I wanted to know whether the recent Julys are really hotter *on average*, or
whether a few memorable hot spells just stand out.

**(B) Variable.** **Daily maximum temperature** (`TMAX`, °F) is a **quantitative, continuous** variable,
although the station records it to the nearest whole degree. Each observation is one July day's highest
temperature. The average of this variable over July days is exactly what NOAA's July normal measures,
so comparing my sample mean to 84.4 °F is a fair comparison.

**(C) Hypothesis in words.** I expect the mean daily high temperature of July days in 2021–2025 to be
**greater than** the 1991–2020 normal of 84.4 °F. I chose the direction *before* looking at any data,
because the question is specifically about hotter Julys.

## 3. Sampling

**(A) and (B) Method.** My population is the **`r nrow(frame_jul)` July days from 2021 to 2025**. I drew a
**simple random sample of n = 30 days** without replacement with the stat-tools **Simple Random Sample**
tool. To repeat it:

1. Save the July days as a CSV with the columns `day_id` (1–155), `date`, `tmax_f` and `tmin_f`.
2. Open the **Simple Random Sample** tool and upload the CSV.
3. Keep all variables, set **Sample size = 30** and **Seed = 251**, and press *Draw sample*.
   The same seed always draws the same 30 days.

```{r, fig.cap="**Figure 1.** The Simple Random Sample tool after the draw: 30 of 155 July days sampled with seed 251. The first rows of the sample are shown.", out.width="90%", fig.align="center"}
include_graphics("example_projects/figs/p2_srs.png")
```

**(C) Justification.**

* **Why SRS.** An SRS gives every July day in all five years the same chance of selection. That keeps me from
  (even unconsciously) picking heat-wave days, and it lets the sample represent all five Julys.
* **Why not a systematic sample.** A systematic sample, such as every 5th day, would be a poor choice here.
  Weather comes in multi-day spells, so evenly spaced days could line up with a repeating pattern.
* **Why not stratify.** I also considered stratifying by year (6 days from each July). That would guarantee
  every year appears equally. The SRS does include all five years, but unevenly: 10 days are from 2021 and
  only 3 from 2024 (see Appendix A). Because the 2021 heat wave might make 2021 unusually hot, I checked.
  The 20 sampled days *outside* 2021 average 90.9 °F, essentially the same as the full sample, so the
  uneven mix does not drive my result. In hindsight, stratifying by year would have been a slightly better
  design.

**Possible bias.**

* **Dependence between nearby days.** Hot days cluster in heat waves, so days that are close together are not
  fully independent. A few of my sampled days are only 1–2 days apart, for example July 27, 29 and 30, 2021.
  If those days fall in the same hot spell, they give slightly less independent information than 30 truly
  separate days would.
* **One station.** Everything describes one station, at one location on campus.

**(D) The sample** is listed in full in [Appendix A](#appendix-a-the-sample).

## 4. Exploratory Statistical Description

**(A) Descriptive statistics** from the stat-tools **Statistic Calculator**, which uses R's default quartile
definition:

```{r}
q <- quantile(x, c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75), type = 7)
desc <- data.frame(
  Statistic = c("minimum", "Q1", "median", "mean", "Q3", "maximum", "interquartile range", "standard deviation"),
  `Value (°F)` = c(sprintf("%.0f", min(x)), sprintf("%.2f", q[1]), sprintf("%.0f", q[2]), sprintf("%.4f", mean(x)),
                   sprintf("%.2f", q[3]), sprintf("%.0f", max(x)), sprintf("%.2f", q[3] - q[1]), sprintf("%.4f", sd(x))),
  check.names = FALSE)
kable(desc, align = c("l", "r"),
      caption = "**Table 1.** Descriptive statistics of the daily maximum temperature for the 30 sampled July days.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"))
```

```{r, fig.cap="**Figure 2.** Statistic Calculator output and boxplot for the 30 sampled daily highs (°F). The red point is the low outlier (68 °F).", out.width="80%", fig.align="center"}
include_graphics("example_projects/figs/p2_summary_boxplot.png")
```

**(B) Plots.** The boxplot is in Figure 2. The histogram below came from the **Make Graphs** tool, with its
automatic bins, which are the same ones R's `hist()` uses:

```{r, fig.cap="**Figure 3.** Histogram of the daily maximum temperature on 30 sampled July days in Moscow, 2021–2025. The bins are 5 °F wide.", out.width="85%", fig.align="center"}
include_graphics("example_projects/figs/p2_histogram.png")
```

**(C) Shape, center and variability.**

* **Shape.** The distribution is **unimodal** and peaks in the 90–95 °F bin. It is **slightly left-skewed**:
  most days fall between 80 and 105 °F, with a short tail toward cooler days. The mean (90.87 °F) sits a
  little below the median (92 °F), which fits a left skew.
* **Center.** The median July high in the sample is **92 °F** and the mean is **90.87 °F**. Both are well
  above the 84.4 °F normal. In fact, 27 of the 30 sampled days were hotter than 84.4 °F.
* **Variability.** The standard deviation is **7.39 °F** and the IQR is **9.75 °F**, so the middle half of the
  days ranged from 86 to 95.75 °F.
* **Outliers.** The lower fence is $Q_1 - 1.5 \cdot IQR = 86 - 1.5(9.75) = 71.375$ °F. **July 4, 2022, at
  68 °F**, falls below it and is an outlier. NOAA gives it no quality flag, and it came during a cool,
  rainy spell (0.54 in of rain fell on July 3 and 0.06 in on July 4). So it is a real observation, not a
  recording error, and I kept it. It pulls the mean *down*, which works *against* my alternative hypothesis. So if anything, keeping
  it makes the test more cautious. I check its influence in Part 5.

## 5. Hypothesis Testing

**(A) Hypotheses.** Let $\mu$ be the mean daily maximum temperature of July days at the Moscow U of I station
in 2021–2025.

\[ H_0: \mu = 84.4 \text{ °F} \qquad\qquad H_a: \mu > 84.4 \text{ °F} \]

In words, $H_0$ says recent July highs average the same as the 1991–2020 normal. $H_a$ says they average
hotter. I use a significance level of **$\alpha = 0.05$**.

**(B) Choice of test and assumptions.** I use a **one-sample $t$ test for a mean**. I have one quantitative
variable and want to compare its mean with a fixed benchmark. The population standard deviation
$\sigma$ is unknown, so I estimate it with $s$, which is why the test uses a $t$ distribution rather than $z$.

The assumptions are:

1. **Random sample.** Satisfied, because the days were chosen by SRS (Part 3).
2. **Independent observations.** Mostly satisfied. The 30 days are spread over five summers, but a few are
   close together (see Part 3), so this is the weakest assumption.
3. **Approximately normal population, or a large enough sample.** The histogram is roughly bell-shaped with a
   mild left skew and one low outlier. With $n = 30$ the Central Limit Theorem makes the sampling
   distribution of $\bar{x}$ approximately normal, so the $t$ test is reasonable.

**(C) Computations.**

*Step 1: observed statistics* (Table 1): $n = 30$, $\bar{x} = 90.8667$ °F, $s = 7.3893$ °F.

*Step 2: standard error.*
\[ SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{7.3893}{\sqrt{30}} = \frac{7.3893}{5.4772} = 1.3491 \text{ °F} \]

*Step 3: test statistic.*
\[ t_{obs} = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}} = \frac{90.8667 - 84.4}{1.3491} = \frac{6.4667}{1.3491} = 4.793 \]

*Step 4: degrees of freedom and critical value.* $df = n - 1 = 29$. For an upper-tail test at
$\alpha = 0.05$ the critical value is $t_{29,\,0.95} = 1.699$, and we reject $H_0$ if $t_{obs} \geq 1.699$.

*Step 5: p-value.* $p = P(t_{29} \geq 4.793) \approx 0.00002$, which the tool reports as $< 0.0001$.

*Step 6: 95% confidence interval for $\mu$* ($t_{29,\,0.975} = 2.045$):
\[ \bar{x} \pm t_{29,\,0.975}\, SE = 90.8667 \pm 2.045(1.3491) = 90.8667 \pm 2.759 = (88.11,\ 93.63) \text{ °F} \]

I ran the test in the stat-tools **One Sample Tests** tool with these settings:

* Mean, hypothesis test, upper tail, $\alpha = 0.05$, $\mu_0 = 84.4$.
* Data: the sample CSV uploaded, with the `tmax_f` column chosen.

It reproduces every value above:

```{r, fig.cap="**Figure 4.** One Sample Tests tool output: SE = 1.3491, df = 29, t = 4.7933, critical value 1.6991, p < 0.0001, and 95% CI (88.1074, 93.6259). The plot shades the rejection region under the null t(29) distribution.", out.width="85%", fig.align="center"}
include_graphics("example_projects/figs/p2_t_test.png")
```

| Quantity | Value |
|:---|---:|
| Sample mean $\bar{x}$ | 90.87 °F |
| Standard error | 1.349 °F |
| Degrees of freedom | 29 |
| Test statistic $t_{obs}$ | 4.793 |
| Critical value $t_{29,\,0.95}$ | 1.699 |
| $p$-value | $< 0.0001$ |
| 95% CI for $\mu$ | (88.11, 93.63) °F |

*Effect of the outlier.* To check the outlier's influence, I removed the 68 °F day and reran the same
$t$ test in R with `t.test()`. That gives $n = 29$, $\bar{x} = 91.66$, $s = 6.10$ and $t = 6.40$, so the
conclusion does not change. The outlier does not drive the result. If anything, including it made the
evidence look weaker.

## 6. Conclusion

**(A) Decision.** The test statistic $t_{obs} = 4.79$ is far beyond the critical value $1.699$, and
$p < 0.0001 < \alpha = 0.05$. So I **reject $H_0$**.

**(B) Interpretation.** There is strong evidence that July days in Moscow from 2021 to 2025 were hotter, on
average, than the 1991–2020 normal. The 95% confidence interval says the average July high in those years was
between about **88.1 and 93.6 °F**. That is roughly **4 to 9 degrees above** the 84.4 °F normal, which is
a difference you would notice outdoors, not just a statistical technicality.

**(C) Limitations.**

* **Five summers is a short window.** This tells us about 2021–2025, not about a long-term trend. A few
  unusually hot summers can happen by chance, and the 2021 heat dome is one example. My result does not
  prove *why* these summers were hot. Separating a climate trend from year-to-year variation would need
  many more years of data.
* **Dependence between days.** Heat waves make nearby days similar. My few close-together sampled days
  make my standard error a bit too small, so the true uncertainty is slightly larger than the interval
  suggests. Still, the evidence is strong enough that this would not change the decision.
* **Finite population.** I sampled 30 of only 155 days (19%). The formulas from class assume a very large
  population, and here that works in the conservative direction.
* **One station.** The result describes the campus station only. Other locations, or changes to this
  station's instruments or surroundings over time, could give different numbers.

## Appendix A: the sample

```{r}
app <- sample_jul[, c("sample_order", "day_id", "date", "tmax_f", "tmin_f")]
names(app) <- c("Draw order", "day_id", "Date", "Daily high (°F)", "Daily low (°F)")
kable(app, align = c("r", "r", "l", "r", "r"),
      caption = "**Table A1.** The 30 July days drawn by the Simple Random Sample tool (seed 251), in the order they were drawn. Only the daily high is analyzed.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"))
```

Days per year in the sample:
`r paste(names(table(substr(sample_jul$date, 1, 4))), " (", table(substr(sample_jul$date, 1, 4)), ")", sep = "", collapse = ", ")`.
